\section{Bureau Visibility and Affordability Screening}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex (results/raw/rq3s.parquet,
% 100 replicates per arm), tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from
% results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py.

This section answers RQ3. The benchmark is the position before the reporting arrangements:
\ac{BNPL} obligations are invisible to the bureau and \ac{BNPL} requests pass only a light
screen. Under bureau visibility, \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's
Regulation 23A test, which is how we model the reported bureau arrangements
\cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}. Under mandatory screening, the same test is applied to every
\ac{BNPL} request, a stricter version of the \ac{FCA}'s affordability check
\cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}. A third arm combines both (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}). Each
arm runs at $\beta=0$ and $\beta=1$ with one hundred replicates on shared seeds, so a
difference of 0.1 points in default is detected about half the time and one of 0.15 points
usually. Whether an agreement that levies late
fees is incidental credit, and which provisions would then apply, is a legal question the
scenarios do not settle.

Neither switch lowers default (Table~\ref{tab:scenarios}; Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}). Bureau
visibility raises it, by $0.22 \pm 0.04$ points at $\beta=0$ and $0.15 \pm 0.04$ at
$\beta=1$. Screening leaves it unchanged, although an effect of about a tenth of a point in
either direction cannot be ruled out.

Bureau visibility works through refusals. Once the lender sees \ac{BNPL} instalments, it
refuses about a sixth more applications and lends 8 to 9\% less. A refused household in the
model has no other source of credit. If its shortfall is in debt service, the instalment goes
unpaid and it is distressed in that tick. A food or rent shortfall is distress either way, but
a granted loan is spent on debt service or saved, which can prevent the next tick's shortfall
(Section~\ref{sec:sequence}). The 90+ share and default rise accordingly, most in Q1, the
poorest quintile, and by less in Q5. \ac{BNPL} volume barely changes, because the switch acts on
traditional lending and not on \ac{BNPL} requests.

The model's rules may favour this result. A refusal can cause distress at once, whereas a granted
loan is repaid over 25 months, partly after the run ends, and the lender assesses surveyed
rather than current income. The switch was not run under the alternative borrowing rules of
Table~\ref{tab:effect} or over a longer horizon. The result gives the direction of the
affordability channel under these rules and does not forecast the effect of the reporting
arrangements.

Screening reduces \ac{BNPL} use only slightly: holding at the final tick falls by two to three
points and volume by 1 to 4\%. Three features of the model may explain why default does not
move. A \ac{BNPL} agreement is small beside the room the Regulation 23A test allows, so the
test refuses only households already near its limit. The test assesses affordability when
credit is granted, whereas sustained distress follows income shocks that arrive later
(Section~\ref{sec:results-robustness}). A shortfall request that screening refuses also passes
in full to the traditional lender (Algorithm~\ref{alg:gate}). None of these explanations is
tested, because the outcomes do not follow screened households.

With both switches, default is 0.10 to 0.11 points above the benchmark: at $\beta=0$,
screening roughly halves the rise in refusals and in default that visibility causes on its
own. A likely reason, not tested, is that screening refuses \ac{BNPL} to households near the
Regulation 23A limit, whose \ac{BNPL} instalments would otherwise lead the traditional lender
to refuse them. Peer influence raises default by
about 0.6 points in every arm but does not detectably change the effect of either switch
($-0.07 \pm 0.06$ points for bureau visibility).

Two further levers, each run at both values of $\beta$, are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:levers}:
a cooling-off window of one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase, and a cap on the number
of platforms a household may owe, which no jurisdiction we found imposes. Neither changes default
detectably at $\beta = 0$; at $\beta = 1$ every window and caps of one and two lower default by
0.28 to 0.39 points. The cap of two lowers default by $0.24 \pm 0.08$ points more than a cap on
agreements that removes as much volume, so lost volume alone does not explain the fall.

In answer to RQ3, making \ac{BNPL} visible to the traditional lender reduces traditional
lending and raises default, most in the poorest quintile, because refused households have
nowhere else to borrow. Mandatory screening slightly reduces \ac{BNPL} borrowing and does not
change default detectably. Under the model's rules neither measure lowers aggregate default.
